title: Physical (electromagnetic) stackup of microphone_array_v2
description: The structure of the four-layer stack, and nothing about its materials.
This file exists because `microphone_array_v2.kicad_pcb` carries no
`(setup (stackup ...))` block at all. KiCad only stores a physical
stackup when a designer fills one in, and this board's was never filled
in, so the board file states the overall thickness (1.6 mm) and the
copper layer order and says nothing about dielectric thickness, material,
relative permittivity or loss tangent.
What is declared here is only what the authoritative board already
establishes: that there are four copper layers in the order F.Cu, In1.Cu,
In2.Cu, B.Cu, and that three dielectrics separate them. That is the
structure. Every material figure is explicitly null.
The nulls are the point. They are not placeholders waiting to be filled
with something plausible - they are the record that this board does not
yet know these values, so that STACK.PHYSICAL can name them one by one
instead of reporting the useless 'no physical stackup at all', and so
that TIMING.INTERCONNECT_DELAY refuses to produce a picosecond figure
rather than producing one derived from an assumed FR-4.
A delay estimate whose Dk was guessed is not a weaker result than one
whose Dk was measured. It is a different kind of thing wearing the same
units, and nothing downstream could tell them apart.
how_to_complete_this_file: Every missing figure comes from one place: the fabricator's stackup
drawing for the ordered service and thickness. For a JLCPCB four-layer
1.6 mm order that is the impedance/stackup document shown at order time
and available afterwards from the order page; it names the prepreg and
core construction, each dielectric thickness, each copper weight, and the
laminate's Dk at a stated frequency.
Record the figures with the same discipline the JLCPCB process profile
requires of a process limit: the source, a URL or document identifier, a
retrieval date, the service and thickness it applies to, and the
frequency the Dk is quoted at. Put those in `provenance` below.
Dk is frequency dependent. The PDM clock is 3.072 MHz with edges an order
or two faster, so a figure quoted at 1 GHz is the appropriate one to use
